messages.subject: power analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I need to conduct some power analyses to assess the statistical power
and/or needed sample size of an annual point count survey to detect changes
in bird density over time.  While there seems to be a wealth of resources
and examples for how to conduct such analyses when the trend is based on
counts, I'm having more trouble finding guidance on how to assess
statistical power and needed sample size when the metric is density, rather
than counts.

Can anyone point me to resources (websites, published papers, etc.) that
might provide some guidance?

Many thanks,
Rodney Siegel

messages.subject: distance sampling of butterflies
messages.body_plain:
I am beginning a study of butterfly density, using transect walks in
forested areas.  I would like to use distance sampling rather than the belt
transects that are traditionally used.  The only example in the Distance
Sampling book of moving objects is seabirds, and I'm wondering if anyone has
implemented the method in the field with butterflies and may have some
advice to share or practical suggestions for sampling.

I'm also interested in incorporating "looking behind" on the transect.  I
believe this may be useful for butterflies as some may not "flush" until
after the observer has passed.  During one of my first surveys this week, an
assistant watched a butterfly fly behind me and over my head.  Had it not
then crossed in front of me, I would have missed it even though it was
directly on the transect line.  However, I'm concerned that by looking
behind I would miss butterflies ahead or increase the chances of
double-counting an individual.  I will not always have the luxury of two
observers in the field, so it would be difficult to rely upon a two-observer
protocol.

Thank you for any ideas or advice,

Amy

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Amy Pocewicz, Ph.D. Candidate

Department of Forest Resources

University of Idaho, Moscow, ID 83844-1133

poce...@uidaho.edu

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

messages.subject: Re: distance sampling of butterflies
messages.body_plain:
Hi Amy,

I have worked out seemingly good distance protocols for butterflies in
alpine environments.  I would be happy to send you excerpts from my
dissertation if you want.  But you seem to have identified the main
points.

1.  Movement.  The usual distance protocols are clear for butterflies that
were initially at rest.  Flying butterflies are more difficult.  I chose
to count butterflies only when the passed through a plane perpendicular to
the transect and at arms-lenght in front of the observer.  Analagous to
"coming astern" in shipboard surveys.  Only counting in this plane also
serves to reduce positive bias incurred if butterfly movement is fast
relative to the observer (this depends on how you measure it).  Counting
butterflies at arms lenght helps one to observe their position before they
respond to the observer.

2.  g0 is very important.  I suggest using something like a net to sweep
the vegetation in front of you on the line, insuring that all butterflies
flush.  Sweep some to the sides as well so that you enforce a decent
shoulder to g(x).  Don't sample in weather that precludes flushing (cold
or wet).  The problem with the "look behind" method is the butterfly has
already moved in response to the observer, a no no.  Continue to evaluate
this assumption with a few double-observer surveys, record the results as
you will be asked about this...

3.  Grouped distances are essential.  Choose bins that are narrow near
observer and wide further away.  I used 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5 m as
cutpoints, pooling groups later if necessary.

4.  FInd a method to reduce error in distance measurment.  I used a 3m rod
marked with the intervals.  Visual estimates are poor.

5.  Plot your data early on and make sure you have a good shape to g(x). I
see a tendency for spiked detection functions unless some effort is made
in the field to enforce a shoulder.  Search the line, but also next to the
line.

6.  Plan for variation in detection probability by observer and habitat.
Butterfly species-specific detection can probably be adequately handled by
pooling speices according to size (small, meduin, large).

I also have some data shared by Leslie Reis (U Northern Arizona) using
point transect for butterflies.  She marked the distance intervals with
flagging on the ground.  It worked well, but lines are still more
effiicent.

A few papers in the area (sorry I don't have citations with me) include
Dave Boughton's (Am Nat?) looking at source-sink dynamics and Boyce and
Brown on the Karner Blue.  Let me know if you can't track them down, I can
find them in my other office.  Neither is an ideal model for distance
sampling of butterflies, but a start nonetheless.

Good luck!!

~aaron

messages.subject: Truncation by prescribed distance or % of observations?
messages.subject_clean: Truncation by prescribed distance or % of observations?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have 105 observations of a rare species surveyed on line transects carried out in varied woodland habitat.  There is one obvious outlier, at 122m from the transect line; the rest of the observations are distributed with a reasonable tail out to 63m (the next largest perpendicular distance).

I want just to remove the 122m obs so...
How can I establish whether truncating at a given distance (120m, 100m, etc.?) or the largest 1% of obs is the most suitable approach?

I feel that this is worth asking since I have tried these options and get very different (although not 'significant') population estimates (ESW's vary between 28.1 and 31.8).

Many thanks in advance for any advice on this.
-Keith.

messages.subject: Re: Truncation by prescribed distance or % of observations?
messages.subject_clean: Truncation by prescribed distance or % of observations?
messages.body_plain:
> > I have 105 observations of a rare species surveyed on line transects
> > carried out in varied woodland habitat.  There is one obvious outlier,
> > at 122m from the transect line; the rest of the observations are
> > distributed with a reasonable tail out to 63m (the next largest
> > perpendicular distance).
> >
> > I want just to remove the 122m obs so...
> > How can I establish whether truncating at a given distance (120m, 100m,
> > etc.?) or the largest 1% of obs is the most suitable approach?
> >
> > I feel that this is worth asking since I have tried these options and
> > get very different (although not 'significant') population estimates
> > (ESW's vary between 28.1 and 31.8).

Keith, if you truncate more, ESW will necessarily reduce, but this doesn't
usually lead to a corresponding increase in the popn abundance estimate
(because encounter rate also reduces as observations are truncated).
However, if you don't truncate sufficiently, odd things can happen if the
model fails to handle the tail of the distribution sensibly.  So for your
data, the largest truncation distance I would even consider using would
be the value of your second largest obsn - 63m (or perhaps say 65m).  Any
larger value, and you're expecting the model to fit the tail of your
distribution but without any data.  Whether it is worth truncating more
than this depends on whether the remaining data exhibit a tail that is
difficult to model.

Steve

messages.subject_clean: Spatial abundance estimation of deer: combining kernel and
messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,

I am working on the last part of my PhD thesis on the ecology and
conservation of two brocket deer species (Mazama americana and M. pandora)
and white-tailed deer in the Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico (Greater Calakmul
Region). I would like to know your opinion on a new technique that I am
trying to develop.

Unfortunatelly, I am not a regular user of Distance sampling for the simple
reason that sightings of these animals in my study area are very
infrequent. For example, in four years of transect work (more that 1200 km
walked) for both direct (sightings) and indirect(tracks, pathways)surveys,
only 62 sightings with accurate information (e. g. correct species id,
perpendicular distances) were made. This does not mean that deer are not
abundant in the area as confirmed by relativelly high abundance indices (as
compared with other areas elsewhere in the Neotropics) and high harvest
rates by local subsistence hunters. Basically, the problem is that close
understory vegetation, high hunting pressure, difficulty in walking quietly
through the forest and overall waryness of deer preclude the use of
observations for abundance/density estimations.

I have been working on a model to predict the spatial abundance of deer in
this area with the combined use of kernel isophlets and transect surveys
with deer signs (tracks/patways)observations.

My survey design was the following:

The information on deer abundance comes from the 46 non-permanent transects
set in a random-stratified fashion over a large study area of about 155
km2. Deer abundance was estimated with the count of deer sign encounter
rates (SER =3D tracks/deer patways/km). During the monitoring of this
transects, sections of 100 meters were marked with flagging tape and
therefore a rough estimate of the exact location of each individual
detection event can be positioned within the length of the transect at 100
meters intervals. Only the transects with no overlapping sampling areas
were chosen for this analysis.

To accomplish this, the following 4 steps were necessary:  (1) The exact
GPS location of the transect and its total length was incorporated into a
GIS line coverage. The habitat gradients that the transect crosses can be
estimated by overlaying the transect with the vegetation map of the study
area (2) The approximated location of deer SER detections events is
digitalized as a point coverage, overlaying the transect coverage using the
information on transect length and the 100 meters sections to pinpoint the
exact location of the detection events.

(3) Because the amount and spatial distribution of detection events can be
extremely variable within the transects in absolute numbers, a rating
system of SER location is used rather than exact numbers. This rating
system uses the following categories to group SER events into point
clusters: =A1=DC 1 deer signs/km =3D 1 point; between 1 to 2 deer signs/km =3D=
 2
points; between 2 to 3 deer signs/km =3D 3 points and =A1=DD 4 deer signs/km=
 =3D 5
points, (4) this rates are considered equivalent to very low, low, moderate
and high abundance of deer signs, respectively and therefore can be
interpreted as an spatial index of relative abundance, where (I argue)that
probabilistic Adaptive Kernel (AK) isophlets can also be estimated using
clustered deer sign groups rather than number of signs. It is argued that
this method provides an accurate picture of deer abundance at the landscape
level when mapped with the AK method in a GIS.

To calculate AK with this information, deer abundance was rated with a 95%
probability or 1 confidence interval (CI) that =A1=DD 5 SER/km will occur;
moderate deer abundance with a 90% probability or 2 CI for 2 to 3 SER/km;
low deer abundance with 85% probability or 3 CI for 2 SER/km and very low
deer abundance with an 80% probability or 5 CI for =A1=DC 1 SER/km. Finally,=
 a
least square validation of the Kernel isophlets is performed and the map
can now be compared with the other methods used for deer abundance
estimation.

My hypthesis is that, the AK provide a spatial representation of the
probability of finding a given deer sign encounter rate per square
kilometre (SER/km2) in a landscape sampled with systematic, random,
stratified transects. This might be interpreted as an indirect method for
the estimation and spatial representation of the relative abundance of deer
in that sampled landscape.

The comparisons of abundance estimates with traditional SER methods and my
model are very similar with the advantage that I can now visualise the
spatial representation of abundance in my study area.

I have found a few references on the combined use of kernel and distance
methods, but all are completelly theoretical (Mack Y, P and Quang P, X.
1998. Kernel methods in line and point transect sampling. Biometrics. 54:
606-619. Mack, Y. P., Quang P. X. and  Zhang, S 1999. Kernel estimation in
transect sampling without the shoulder condition. Communications in
statistics theory and methods. 28: 2277-2296). So far, I have been unable
to find any empirical study on the use of these two methods.

Now, my main questions for you guys in the list are three:

1. As I understand from the literature, a kernel estimate provides a direct
density estimate that can be interpreted as a Utilization Distribution
function. Is it "safe" to assume that the utilization distribution (UD)
estimate from Kernel methods provides and accurate spatial representation
of the abundance in this case and with this design?

2. I have been looking for methods to validate my model. Unfortunatelly I
have no abundance estimation other than SER, but I do have GPS locations of
deer kills by hunters (92 in total over the same four years period)that I
am using to estimate the spatial and temporal patterns of deer hunters. Can
you think of a way where I can compare these two independent data-sets to
validate my kernel-transect model?

3. Is there anybody out there that you may know who might have used kernel-
tansect methods in a similar fashion?

Thanks a lot for your input and sorry for the long message.
Regards

Manuel
_________________________________
Manuel Weber, DVM, M.Sc
PhD Student
Ecology Group
School of Biological and Biomedical Sciences
University of Durham, Durham UK
and
El Colegio de la Frontera Sur-ECOSUR
Campeche, Mexico.

There is a short section on power analysis for estimating trends in the
chapter "Temporal inferences from distance sampling surveys" from the
up-coming book "Advanced Distance Sampling".  The book is due out this
summer; I can email you a copy of the chapter if you can't wait (and
anyone else who's interested).  I also have some practical step-by-step
examples (using Tim Gerrodette's TRENDS) for simplistic scenarios

inferences I gave at the last Introduction to Distance Sampling workshop.
Again, I can email these.  Lastly, there was a thread on this group quite
recently about appropriate the CV-density relationship to use.

Others may know of more resources.  In any case, hope this helps,

 - Len Thomas

messages.subject: repeat visits, pseudoreplication,
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

In a study of wintering grassland birds, I laid out 8 permanent transect
lines. There are usually few birds detected per visit, so I visited the
same lines several times to increase sample sizes. This is discussed in
Introduction to Distance Sampling on page 294 and elsewhere. The book
states that the data can be pooled from these visits to increase sample
size, as long as the line length is multiplied by the number of visits. My
transects are 1km long. I want to get my detection function using data
from all 8 transects (they are all in the same area/habitat), and get
density estimates for each transect line based on pooled data from all
visits.

My problem is that some people in my department with better statistical
knowledge than I say that pooling observations from multiple visits to the
same transect line constitutes pseudoreplication. They point out that some
of these species are territorial in the winter, therefore if that bird is
detected at a certain distance from the line on visit 1, it will probably
be detected there (or close by) on subsequent visits. They contend that I
cannot pool data from multiple visits.

I have heard this argument from other people, all of whom are more
statistically adept than I. Therefore it is hard to counter their
arguments with anything other than "the book says it's ok". If these
people are doubtful then I'm sure others (i.e. reviewers) will be too. I
myself am starting to wonder. Why is it alright to pool? I need an
explanation simple enough for my statistically-challenged mind to
understand, but also enough to convince these people that pooling is
appropriate in my case. Any advice is greatly appreciated.

Regards,
Joe Roberts
Department of Zoology
University of Oklahoma

messages.subject: Re: repeat visits, pseudoreplication,
messages.body_plain:
I will take a crack at this, but I will also be interested in what the big
guns can add...

First recall that there are (in this case) two levels of estimation:

1. Estimate encounter rate and its variance.  The sample units here are
the individual lines.  Following the strategy you outlined, sample size is
not inflated by your repeated counts and no psuedoreplication worries
arise.  Here n=8 which is small.  Variance in encounter rate may be high,
and you might worry about meeting the assumption that distances are
uniform...

2.  Estimate detection probability (Pa) and its variance.  This is where
the criticisms come in.  Sample units are individual detections.  The
critical assumption is that detections are independent.  The fact that birds are in similar locations does not by
itself induce dependence.  The only problem is if the observer introduces
dependence by recalling, for example, that "there is a male meadow lark
that I saw on that fence post last time and I want to make sure I count
him again."  The fact that there is still a bird at postion Y does not
mean the act of detecting the bird is dependent on previous detections. In
fact, there are no assumptions made at all about the distribution of birds
as long as the lines are randomly placed.

This last point is admittedly subtle.  Imagine a case where the objects
(eg, stakes) do not move at all.  Assuming the observer does not rely on
memory to find stakes, detections on repeated counts are still
independent.  That is, whether or not stake Y is detected depends only on
its distance (and maybe other covariates), not whether it was previously
detected.  Movement is not required.  The fact that birds do move some
between surveys only helps to insure distances really are uniformly
distributed (especially since you only have 8 lines).

What say, mates?

~aaron

messages.subject: Re: repeat visits, pseudoreplication,
messages.body_plain:
Below is the message I sent to Joe and I'll resend here to the list.  I
do agree with everything that Aaron says although with 8 lines there may
be some difficulty in assuring that distances are uniform relative to
the line. Even if the detections are independent between visits, if the
object is in the same place each time I would not handle it in the same
way. If the birds move say >1/2 W then this will provide more assurance.

Joe-
It would be psuedo-replication if you treated each visit to the line as
if it was an independent sample.  But if you properly treat it as a
single sample (as described on pg 294), then by repeating visits you are
just geting a better estimate of density on that line. It is somewhat
equivalent to making multiple measurements of a pig's weight to reduce
measurement error of your scale. In the analysis you would end up using
the average weight for the each pig as a sample. And your sample size
would be the number of pigs.  Now it isn't quite equivalent because you
may be using the fitted detection function across lines. But the primary
source of variance is due to the number of objects seen per unit line
length (here we mean line length*visits).  For that variance you are
using numbers of lines as the sample size and not numbers of
line-visits. Now with regard to the argument that because it is land a
bird may be in the same position.  Possibly but unlikely.  The only
thing that matter here is perpendicular distance.  If birds only moved
say less than 1/2 the width of your transect perpendicular to your line
then I'd be worried, but I don't think that is likely even if they are
territorial but you are the best judge of that.  It would be a different
story if the objects were immobile.  Then their position with regard to
the line wouldn't change and it would be incorrect to pool as we
describe but replicate surveys of immobile objects could be treated in a
mark-recapture setting so even then multiple visits would be
appropriate.  Because inter-transect variability is the primary source
of variance, unless the objects are immobile I wouldn't worry about the
comments of your colleagues.  If they have any further questions, have
them contact me directly. They probably think that you are treating each
visit to the line as a separate sample which would be innapropriate.

regards--jeff

> > lines. There are usually few birds detected per visit, so I visited the
> > same lines several times to increase sample sizes. This is discussed in
> > Introduction to Distance Sampling on page 294 and elsewhere. The book
> > states that the data can be pooled from these visits to increase sample
> > size, as long as the line length is multiplied by the number of visits. My
> > transects are 1km long. I want to get my detection function using data
> > from all 8 transects (they are all in the same area/habitat), and get
> > density estimates for each transect line based on pooled data from all
> > visits.
> >
> > My problem is that some people in my department with better statistical
> > knowledge than I say that pooling observations from multiple visits to the
> > same transect line constitutes pseudoreplication. They point out that some
> > of these species are territorial in the winter, therefore if that bird is
> > detected at a certain distance from the line on visit 1, it will probably
> > be detected there (or close by) on subsequent visits. They contend that I
> > cannot pool data from multiple visits.
> >
> > I have heard this argument from other people, all of whom are more
> > statistically adept than I. Therefore it is hard to counter their
> > arguments with anything other than "the book says it's ok". If these
> > people are doubtful then I'm sure others (i.e. reviewers) will be too. I
> > myself am starting to wonder. Why is it alright to pool? I need an
> > explanation simple enough for my statistically-challenged mind to
> > understand, but also enough to convince these people that pooling is
> > appropriate in my case. Any advice is greatly appreciated.
> >
> > Regards,
> > Joe Roberts
> > Department of Zoology
> > University of Oklahoma

messages.subject: Re: repeat visits, pseudoreplication,
messages.body_plain:
Just to add briefly to Aaron and Jeff's comments:  as Aaron notes, it is
the variance component corresponding to fitting the detection function
that could be impacted.  This tends to be the smaller component, and the
effect tends to be small.  However, with several revisits to the same
lines, if birds often used say a favorite songpost, you might see a very
small effect on variance, and a slight tendency to fit too many adjustment
terms - model selection will be affected by the overdispersion in the
data.  A simple way around the variance estimation bias is to use the
bootstrap option, resampling 'samples' (i.e. lines).  This treats the 8
lines as independent samples, and detections on the same line need not be
independent.  My main concern would not be related to repeated visits, but
whether 8 lines are sufficient for reliable inference.  If the habitat is
fairly homogeneous and bird density does not vary greatly between lines,
it may be not too bad.

Steve

messages.subject: Re: Question about the line-transect using program-DISTANCE
messages.subject_clean: Question about the line-transect using program-DISTANCE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daisuke, list,

There is no requirement that the lines should be parallel.  See Introduction to
Distance Sampling, section 7.2.1 for a discussion of this, and Figure 7.3 for some
examples of square transects.  There can be some issues with what to do at the
corners -- see the above section and Figure 7.4.

If each each sampler (square, triangle, etc) is placed at random (or, better,
systematic random) then each sampler should be treated as 1 transect in Distance
(ie line length for a square sampler would be the total length of the 4 sides).

 - Len
